FINALLY you compare to native TAA. These videos were a bit null because you rarely compare against proper native presentation, which should be the ideal the sclaers strive to mat ch. Although TAA is shit in 80% of games with too much blur and over accumilation of frames. I hope you in the future do a short video where you compare against 4x SSAA, or 8K super resolution downsampled to 4K (no AA applied, not even TAA, as you want pure anti alisain g and none of the detail removing that TAA does). Yes in motion this comparison isn't super useful because the framerate will be too low, but it should show a "ground truth" example of how the best possible and CORRECT anti aliasaed image looks like.
The closer an upscaler gets to this 4x SSAA, the better it is, if it has too many AI hallicinated details and such, then that makes it miss the mark.
When you comapre AI upscaler to AI upscaler, it inherently normalizes the flaws that these upscalers have, so while you can't game with SSAA, it still important to include to show what the game would look like with abaseloute zero flaws.

The comparison might be easier done at 1080p or 1440p, where the downsampling is less taxing on the GPU.

Still I hope you'll do this, because in the many years of analysing DLSS since the 1.0 days, you've never ever compared to such an example yet.

text:
The RTX has a couple of more features that AMD can't quite match. 

One is the video encoder. Video captured on the RX 9060 XT can look as good as video captured on the RTX 5060 Ti, but it does so at using a higher bitrate and thus the video files will be a bit bigger. AMD has improved the encoder and the software part, but they are still not as good as the nVidia encoder or even the one Intel has. But there are other reasons people use or don't use the Intel graphics cards. Next gen might change that a lot. But for now they are not really competing with these two so I won't mentioning them again for now.

Another is the NVIDIA Broadcast utility. I can't really say anything about the camera features, as I don't have a camera on my computer. But the noise removal feature for audio really works disturbingly well.

Then there's their snapshot utility. I can't even remember what it's called, and it only works in a few games as far as I know. It does work in Tom Clancy's Ghost Recon Wildlands. Using it you freeze the game and enters a feature that allows you to reposition the camera, change zoom, select to emulate different photographic film and so on. It's not something I have used a lot, but I know there are people that love using it and can produce pretty fantastic pictures of games. You can also choose to render the snapshot in super high resolution to get that last bit of quality out of it. I think it also works in The Division.

There's also a feature that allow you to change the color temperature of the game, but I think AMD has something similar, though I don't know if it's a driver feature like what Nvidia does or if it's something you adjust outside of the game.

Now for most gamers I doubt these are things they use every day or would have a problem giving up, and not even essential for enjoyment of the games, but they are there with any RTX card so think what you want about it.

What motherboard? You need B550 or X570 to get pcie4x16 on a 5600. Don't bother with the 5600x just get the 5600 (great chip, had several).
1) enable PBO, 2) set 120w PPT, 3) set Frequency offset +200Mhz, 4) set curve optimiser to -20 on each core then use PBO2tuner and prime95 to test lower and lower negative offsets.

5600: I've had 4 and they all did -30 all core at +200

Edit: ALSO early B0 silicon is very different to later C0, the early chips have a rapid clock drop off as you load cores, C0 keep clocks high right until you hit a power cap which you should just raise.
5950x: had 2 (couldn't use +200) but did crack 30K on CBr23 on air, amazing workhorses.
5800x3D: was hot and not worth it for me but I'm a hardware tester not a FPS addict.

Well, maybe it is AMD that has to work closer with these AAA-Publishers and Game Engine Companies to make Radeon Drivers work better on their hardware.

That's what Nvidia does, they spend a lot of time, effort, and money, to polish their CUDA drivers with the major studios. It's one of the main reasons why the GeForce cards are released with higher efficiency, and punch above their weight class in terms of silicon.
